title: XCENA MX1 CXL Computational Memory Device at Hot Chips 2026 with Samsung
gist: At Hot Chips 2026, XCENA (with Samsung) presented the MX1, a Samsung-Foundry-4nm CXL Type 3 device fusing 2TB DDR5 memory expansion, SSD-backed byte-addressable 'Infinite Memory', and near-memory compute on 3,072 RISC-V cores — arguing the AI bottleneck is memory, not compute, and showing 3.35x LLM decode throughput gains at 100K context via GPU+PNM hybrid attention.

insights.claim: XCENA's core pitch is that AI workloads stall on memory capacity, bandwidth, and power efficiency before they stall on raw compute, so the fix can reside in a CXL device rather than a larger host CPU or faster GPU.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Supports a computational-memory/CXL investment theme distinct from the GPU trade; watch CXL device vendors and memory makers as AI capex diversifies beyond accelerators.
insights.quote: AI workloads stall on memory capacity, bandwidth, and power efficiency before they stall on raw compute.
insights.locator: XCENA MX1 CXL Computational Memory Device at Hot Chips 2026

insights.claim: Samsung stated on stage at Hot Chips 2026 that CXL is being adopted by all the major hyperscalers for workloads like databases and AI/KV cache, signaling CXL is moving from research to hyperscale deployment.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A direct demand signal for the CXL supply chain (memory vendors, switch makers, controller vendors) from a tier-1 memory supplier's own claim.
insights.quote: Samsung just said on stage that CXL is being adopted by all the major hyperscalers for things like databases and AI/ KV cache.
insights.locator: This second half of the session shifts

insights.claim: Samsung's processing-near-memory rationale is bandwidth asymmetry: DDR5 behind the CXL interconnect offers 268.8GB/s versus only 64GB/s on a PCIe Gen6 x8 host link, so computing in place and moving only reduced data beats shipping raw data to the host.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The compute-where-the-data-lives framework generalizes; interconnect bandwidth gaps are the structural moat for near-memory compute products.

insights.claim: The XCENA MX1 is a CXL Type 3 device built on Samsung Foundry's 4nm process that fuses three functions in one package: CXL memory expansion up to 2TB over four DDR5-8400 channels, SSD storage exposed as byte-addressable CXL memory, and near-memory processing on 3,072 custom RISC-V cores.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Real 4nm silicon (not a paper spec) validates the computational-memory category and gives Samsung Foundry an AI-adjacent logic win.

insights.claim: XCENA deliberately chose thousands of simple in-order RISC-V cores over fewer large cores because its target workloads are bandwidth-bound and power-sensitive, and the open RISC-V ISA allows custom instructions for in-memory analytics, RAG retrieval, and memory compression.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Another commercial design win for RISC-V in datacenter accelerators — evidence the open ISA is displacing Arm/proprietary cores in domain-specific silicon.

insights.claim: MX1 organizes its die into 24 subsystems (each four clusters of 32 memory units, 3,072 MUs total, sharing a 128MB L3), with the subsystem as the unit of host job allocation so each can run an independent job; a Vector Processing Engine adds roughly 3 TFLOPS of peak dot-product throughput per SoC aimed at RAG vector search and KV cache scoring.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Multi-tenant job partitioning plus vector primitives shows the part is designed for cloud rental economics, not just single-workload demos.

insights.claim: MX1 lets host and device share a single virtual address space so pointer-rich data structures traverse safely and existing malloc-based code can move to CXL memory with minimal change, while a CXL-aware allocator keeps per-tenant page tables for isolation.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Low software-porting friction is the historical killer of accelerators; shared virtual addressing directly attacks the adoption barrier.
insights.locator: One of the more important software decisions

insights.claim: XCENA reports analytics-kernel throughput up to 4.7x versus host-over-CXL and 2x versus local DRAM at roughly a quarter of host power, for efficiency gains up to 18.7x versus CXL and 6.2x versus DRAM, benchmarked against an Intel Xeon 6767P (idle power excluded).
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Vendor-supplied and idle-power-excluded, but if the ~6-19x efficiency claims hold, near-memory compute undercuts CPU-based analytics on power-constrained datacenter economics.

insights.claim: Samsung reports 10 CXL-PNM devices delivering 64x higher queries per second and 65x better query-per-energy than a host CPU with a CXL memory pool on RAG vector search, using FAISS IVF Flat over a 512M-vector index drawn from Laion 5B, by offloading the memory-bandwidth-bound L2 kNN distance computation.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: RAG retrieval at scale is a fast-growing inference cost center; a 64x QPS claim makes PNM a credible threat to CPU-based vector search infrastructure.

insights.claim: Samsung's headline result: at 100K context, GPU-plus-PNM hybrid attention raises LLM decode throughput 3.35x (17.7 vs 5.50 tokens/sec) and tokens-per-energy 3.84x (4.31 vs 1.12 tokens/kJ), running LLaMA-3.1-70B INT8 across two servers each with five MX1 devices and NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell GPUs.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Long-context inference is where KV cache costs explode; a 3-4x throughput/energy gain at 100K context is the concrete economic case for PNM in inference fleets.
insights.locator: Samsung's results on the hybrid decode

insights.claim: In hybrid attention, the PNM device computes attention on KV-cache miss pages locally and returns only the computed attention result instead of shipping KV pages back to the GPU, while hit pages stay on the GPU.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The mechanism — moving results, not data — is the reusable pattern that determines whether PNM economics generalize beyond this demo.

insights.claim: MX1's 'Infinite Memory' presents SSD capacity as byte-addressable CXL memory via a DRAM-plus-NAND hybrid where DRAM caches 64KB SSD pages tracked by a 1024-entry map-cache TLB, with misses filled by firmware running on the MU cores.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: NAND-backed CXL memory could shift memory-tier economics — watch it as a partial successor to the niche Optane vacated and a volume driver for NAND in AI systems.

insights.claim: Kennedy notes Infinite Memory is essentially a memory-tiering solution seen a few times over the years with XCENA's spin, invoking the death of Intel Optane — a caution that this category has repeatedly failed to commercialize.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Temper enthusiasm: memory tiering has a graveyard (Optane); the open question is whether CXL plus the AI KV-cache use case changes the adoption math this time.
insights.quote: It is basically a memory tiering solution we have seen a few times over the years, with XCENA’s spin on it. If you are wondering, this is probably a good point in the presentation to bemoan the death of Optane.

insights.claim: For KV cache on SSD-backed memory, a pinned prefix keeps query TTFT at just 1.13x DRAM (vs 1.57x unpinned and 1.86x raw SSD), and a lookahead prefetch exploiting device underutilization delivers nearly DRAM-resident performance — tested with Llama-3.1-8B, vLLM, LMCache, and an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Pro.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: If NAND can serve KV cache at near-DRAM latency, inference operators can swap expensive DRAM/HBM capacity for cheap flash — a margin lever and a NAND demand story.

insights.claim: Samsung and XCENA sketched a rack-scale CXL computational memory reference appliance pairing a Liqid CXL switch with GPU servers using 96GB NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell parts, targeting 20TB of pooled memory at 2.7TB/s of bandwidth shared via CXL memory semantics.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Names the emerging rack-scale CXL bill of materials — switch vendors like Liqid and pooled-memory appliances are the picks-and-shovels layer to watch.
insights.locator: Samsung and XCENA sketch a rack-scale

insights.claim: Samsung is pushing a vendor-agnostic near-data-computing software stack: its NDC API is open-sourced through OCP FTI DCC and routes PyTorch through OpenXLA and PrivateUse1 so AI frameworks reach XCENA's PXL runtime without code changes; XCENA itself ships PXL, a MapReduce-style runtime with C/C++ or Rust kernels.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Open, framework-transparent software is how PNM avoids the accelerator software-lock-in trap; OCP standardization would let the category scale beyond one vendor.

insights.claim: The Samsung reference design's use of a PCIe Gen6 x8 host link suggests the system is timed for the just-launching generation of Gen6 server CPUs, implying near-term rather than distant productization.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A timing read: computational-memory appliances could ship into the Gen6 server refresh cycle rather than a later generation.
insights.quote: Maybe the Gen6 x8 link gives away the timing of this since we are just starting to see Gen6 server CPUs launch.

insights.claim: Kennedy's takeaway is that XCENA and Samsung are positioning MX1 as real silicon at the heart of a computational-memory wave, pointing to a memory tier that scales capacity and compute together instead of separately.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: If memory tiers absorb compute, value migrates from host CPUs toward memory vendors and CXL device makers — a structural shift in the server BOM.
insights.quote: a memory tier that scales capacity and compute together
